orgaos-e-sistemas/conceitos-gerais/membr.descricaoOriginal: All surfaces of the body are covered and protected by a membrane, usually consisting of an epithelium and an underlying connective tissue. This diagrammatic cross section through the abdomen illustrates the location of the three types of body membranes: cutaneous, mucous and serous.

base.alt: Fotomicrografia de Membranes — Órgãos e Sistemas › Conceitos Gerais › Membranas › Membranes 1.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: The cutaneous membrane, or skin, covers the exterior of the body and is composed of a stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, called the epidermis, and a connective tissue layer, the dermis.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Cutaneous membrane em Membranes.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: The mucous membrane, or mucosa, lines the lumens of all organs opening directly or indirectly to the exterior of the body, such as the stomach, intestines, trachea, and ureter. Typically, the mucosa is composed of three layers: an epithelium, a connective tissue layer called the lamina propria, and a muscularis mucosae (literally, “muscle of the mucosa”) of smooth muscle.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Mucous membrane em Membranes.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: A serous membrane, or serosa, lines the three internal cavities that do not open to the exterior: pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal cavities. This membrane is composed of simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium) and an underlying connective tissue. During development, at least one organ protrudes into each cavity, pushing serosa ahead of itself as it does so, similar to shoving a fist into the wall of a balloon. Consequently, the serosa lines the outer perimeter of each cavity, as well as being reflected over the outside of the organ protruding into the cavity.

orgaos-e-sistemas/conceitos-gerais/membr.descricaoOriginal: A mucosal membrane (mucosa) lines the lumen of organ systems that open to the exterior of the body (digestive, respiratory and genitourinary). Mucosae are the most highly variable type of membrane, reflecting the diverse functions of the organs in which they are located. A mucosa typically consists of an epithelium, a connective tissue (lamina propria), and a layer of smooth muscle (muscularis mucosae). A mucous membrane is so named because mucus-producing glands frequently secrete onto its surface, providing lubrication. This image shows a section of the small intestine. 100x

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: A loose connective tissue stroma is present beneath the surface epithelium and surrounding the glands. The gelatinous ground substance of this stroma provides good padding for the epithelium, supports the glands and allows for diffusion and cell migration. Delicate collagen fibers are the predominant fiber type in this stroma.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: The stroma also provides more robust structural support for organs wall. In these areas, thick collagen fibers of the dense connective tissue predominate. orgaos-e-sistemas/conceitos-gerais/strom.descricaoOriginal: These images compare the structure of a lymph node stained by the silver method (left) and H&E (right). The stroma of a lymph node is composed of reticular fibers which are specifically stained by the silver technique. The parenchymal tissue is revealed with the H&E stain. The parenchymal cells, mostly lymphocytes, are suspended along a meshwork of reticular fibers that provide delicate support while allowing for cell migration and lymph passage. The reticular fibers are not differentiated by the H&E stain. 100x.

orgaos-e-sistemas/conceitos-gerais/strom.descricaoOriginal: Organs are made up of two basic components: the functional cells and tissues, termed parenchyma, and a supportive framework, called stroma. orgaos-e-sistemas/conceitos-gerais/tissu.descricaoOriginal: Some organs are not usually thought of as organs, but because they are formed by two or more tissues, they are truly organs. Bone, skin and blood vessels fall into this category. 100x, 100x, 400x

base.alt: Fotomicrografia de Organs — Órgãos e Sistemas › Conceitos Gerais › Tissues and organs 4.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Bone is an organ because it is composed of several types of connective tissue (the tissue bone, bone marrow, and a connective tissue covering), blood vessels (composed of epithelium and muscle), and nerves.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Osso em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Skin is composed of an epidermis of epithelial tissue and a dermis of connective tissue. Blood vessels and nerves supply the skin.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Pele em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Blood vessels, like this medium artery, are lined by an epithelium and have a wall composed of muscle and connective tissue. Vessels may even have their own blood and nerve supplies, although neither is visible here.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Artéria em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Two of these organs have a free surface which, therefore, is lined by an epithelium. The free surface of the skin is the exterior surface of the body and the free surface of the artery is the lumen through which blood flows.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Epitélio em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Several types of connective tissue are found in these three organs. One type, connective tissue proper, forms a covering for bone, the dermis of skin, the hypodermis beneath the skin, and part of the wall of the artery.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Tecido conjuntivo propriamente dito em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Bone, another type of connective tissue, has a firm, calcified matrix that gives bone its rigidity. Bone cells are present within the matrix and on the bone surface.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Osso em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: The spaces within bone are filled with another type of connective tissue called bone marrow.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Medula óssea em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Muscle is a frequent component of organs and forms a majority of the arterial wall. Muscle also forms an important component in the walls of hollow organs, as seen in the previous image. Muscle is absent in bone, except in the walls of the vessels supplying the bones; except for a band of muscle attached to hair follicles, muscle is also absent in skin.

midia.alt: Camada de marcação destacando Músculo em Organs.

overlays.explicacaoOriginal: Blood vessels supply all three of these organs, although they are only visible here in the sections of bone and skin.
